The chase ends on the cursed lake, where Alizayd is dragged into the water. The marid, the water spirits who cursed the lake long ago, take hold of him and use his body, and the possessed Ali kills Dara. Nahri is brought back to the palace with nothing left to bargain with. She heals Ali of what the marid did to him, and Ghassan buries the truth about the possession, then marries her to his heir Muntadhir immediately, binding the Nahid line to the Qahtanis. Ali is sent away to the Geziri provinces in disgrace, an assignment his family does not expect him to survive. Nahri ends the book a queen in name, isolated, grieving, and with no illusions left about the man who brought her east. The epilogue overturns all of it. Far from the city, Dara wakes: pulled out of a quiet afterlife into a body that is whole, freed of the ifrit's slave curse, and restored to the unbound magic his people held before Suleiman's punishment. Two people are standing over him. One is Kaveh e-Pramukh, Daevabad's grand wazir. The other is Banu Manizheh, the Nahid healer everyone believes the ifrit murdered two decades ago. She is alive, she has been preparing for a generation, and she tells Dara that Nahri is her daughter.
recaps.in_short: Nahri is a young con artist and thief in Ottoman Cairo with a healing gift she cannot explain. Performing a ceremony for money, she accidentally summons Darayavahoush, a daeva warrior who tells her she carries the blood of the Nahids, a family of magical healers, and that her only safe place is Daevabad, a hidden djinn city. Hunted by ifrit, the two cross half the world to reach it. There Nahri is received by the Daeva tribe as their Banu Nahida and installed in the palace of King Ghassan al Qahtani, whose ancestors took the city from hers. She befriends the king's younger son, Ali, a devout prince secretly funding the city's despised part-human shafit, and learns that Dara is remembered by the other tribes as the Scourge of Qui-zi, the author of a massacre. To buy protection, Nahri bargains a betrothal to Ghassan's heir, Muntadhir. When Dara tries to take her out of the city, the escape ends in bloodshed on the cursed lake: the marid seize Ali and use him to kill Dara. Nahri is married to Muntadhir and Ali is exiled. In the epilogue Dara wakes restored to life by Banu Manizheh, the Nahid healer believed dead for twenty years, who reveals that Nahri is her daughter.

recaps.text: Nahri makes a living in Ottoman Cairo as a thief and an unlicensed healer, telling fortunes and staging ceremonies she is certain are pure theatre. She hides a genuine gift: she senses illness by touch, and her own wounds close in moments. During a zar she is paid to hold for a girl named Baseema, she sings in a language she cannot identify, and two things answer. One is an ifrit, an ancient and malevolent being that takes hold of the girl. The other is Darayavahoush, a daeva warrior who arrives in a sandstorm, destroys the creatures hunting her and tells her that her blood is not human. He names her a descendant of the Nahids, a family of magical healers, and says the only place she will be safe is Daevabad, a hidden city far to the east. With ifrit behind them and the dead rising from the ground to follow, the two flee Egypt together.

Traveling east by conjured carpet, by boat and on foot, Dara teaches Nahri what she is. Long ago the prophet Suleiman punished the daevas for meddling with humanity, stripped their magic and returned it altered, splitting them into six tribes: the Daevas, who kept the old name, and the Geziri, Ayaanle, Sahrayn, Agnivanshi and Tukharistani. Those who refused to submit became the ifrit, unchanged and cursed, and they take their revenge by enslaving djinn into rings and by hunting the Nahids, the healer family entrusted with Suleiman's seal. Daevabad itself was taken from the Nahids fourteen centuries ago by Zaydi al Qahtani, and his descendants rule it still. Children of mixed human and djinn blood, the shafit, are confined and despised there. Dara served the Nahids as their Afshin, their warrior, and he speaks of the Qahtanis with open hatred. In Daevabad, meanwhile, Prince Alizayd, the king's younger son, trains to command his brother's army while secretly funding a shafit organization his father would call treason.

The journey grows steadily more dangerous. Ifrit ambush them, ghouls follow their trail, and after one attack a peri named Khayzur finds the pair near death and heals them, breaking his own people's rule against interfering. Nahri presses Dara about the gaps in his history and learns that he spent centuries as an ifrit's slave, passed from one human master to the next, with almost no memory of any of it, before he was freed into a world that had moved on without him. In Daevabad, Ali's payments to the Tanzeem are traced. Its leader, Sheikh Anas, is arrested and publicly executed, taking the blame alone and leaving Ali alive, shaken, and further into the shafit cause than before. Nahri and Dara reach the Gozan river, pass through the veil that hides the road, and come within sight of a city of brass on an island in a cursed lake.

Nahri enters Daevabad as the first Nahid healer in twenty years and is received by her own tribe as their Banu Nahida. King Ghassan installs her in the palace, sets her to work in the infirmary under Nisreen, a Daeva woman who served the previous Nahids, and assigns Ali to tutor her. The two become unlikely friends. Dara's return is far less welcome: to the Geziri he is a war criminal, and he is kept under guard and watched. Nahri finds the city's politics as ruthless as any Cairo street. The Daeva tribe, led by grand wazir Kaveh, wants her as their symbol; the Qahtanis want her contained; the shafit, whose conditions appall her, want a healer willing to treat them; and Nahri's rounded ears mark her as carrying human blood, which almost everyone has an opinion about.

Nahri learns what Dara kept from her. During the war that ended Nahid rule he carried out a massacre at Qui-zi, killing and enslaving its shafit population, and the other tribes remember him as the Scourge. He does not deny it, and his presence makes both of them targets. To buy protection for herself, for the Daeva tribe and for Dara, Nahri negotiates a betrothal to the emir Muntadhir, treating her own marriage as a contract to be haggled over. Ali, drawn back into shafit politics by a Royal Guard officer named Rashid, discovers that the money he handed over bought weapons as well as bread. The fallout costs lives, destroys what remains of his father's trust in him, and leaves him with no clean way out of anything.

The city's tensions come apart. Violence between Daeva and shafit escalates, and Ali, stripped of his standing, is caught between the brother he loves and the cause he cannot abandon. Dara, unwilling to leave Nahri in Qahtani hands and unwilling to accept her marriage, presses her to run with him and raise the Daeva against the king. Nahri, who has spent the whole book refusing to be anyone's property or anyone's banner, has to choose between a bargain she made with her eyes open and the man who brought her here, knowing that whichever she picks, people she has treated will pay for it.

Nahri agrees to go with Dara, and the escape turns into a slaughter. Dara cuts through the guards sent to stop them, and Jamshid is gravely wounded by his arrows. The chase ends on the cursed lake, where Ali is pulled into the water. The marid, the water spirits who cursed the lake long ago, take hold of him and use his body: Ali rises marid-possessed and kills Dara. Nahri is returned to the palace, and Dara's ring is taken from the water. Ali is left dying of what the marid did to him, and Nahri heals him, though Ghassan buries the truth about what took him. The king then makes his terms plain, and Nahri is married to Muntadhir at once. Ali is sent away to the Geziri provinces in disgrace, an assignment few expect him to survive.

In the epilogue, Dara wakes. He is pulled out of a quiet afterlife and back into a whole body, freed of the ifrit's slave curse and restored to the full, unbound magic his people held before Suleiman's punishment. He is not alone. Standing over him are Kaveh e-Pramukh, Daevabad's grand wazir, who has spent the entire book at the king's side, and Banu Manizheh, the Nahid healer the world believes the ifrit murdered twenty years ago. She is alive. She has been preparing for a very long time. And she tells Dara that Nahri is her daughter.

characters.description: A veteran homicide detective newly reinstated with the LAPD after three years in retirement. Assigned to the Open-Unsolved Unit, Bosch returns with his old instincts intact but must work inside current rules and prove that coming back was more than nostalgia for the badge.
characters.name: Harry Bosch

characters.description: Bosch's partner in the Open-Unsolved Unit and a detective he has long trusted. Rider combines familiarity with his methods and a stronger regard for the department's present structure as they reopen a murder that was mishandled seventeen years earlier.
characters.name: Kizmin Rider

characters.description: A sixteen-year-old girl taken from her home and found shot in 1988. Rebecca was the daughter of a Black mother and a white father, and the old investigation considered whether racism, her private relationships, or someone close to the family made her a target.
characters.name: Rebecca Verloren

characters.description: Rebecca's father. The unsolved murder helped destroy both his marriage and the life he knew, and the return of detectives forces him to revisit the house, the gun, and the people around his daughter in 1988.
characters.name: Robert Verloren

characters.description: Rebecca's mother. Years of grief and the failure of the original case have left lasting damage, making the reopened inquiry both a possibility of truth and a threat to the limited stability she has recovered.
characters.name: Muriel Verloren

characters.description: A man identified when modern DNA testing matches blood preserved on the murder weapon. His history and associations make him a central suspect, but Bosch and Rider still have to determine how his blood reached the gun and what part he played in Rebecca's death.
characters.name: Roland Mackey

characters.description: The lieutenant supervising the Open-Unsolved Unit. Pratt gives Bosch and Rider the old Verloren file and expects a case built to present standards, not merely an experienced detective's certainty about what went wrong in 1988.
characters.name: Abel Pratt

characters.description: A senior LAPD official and Bosch's longstanding institutional adversary. Irving treats Bosch's return as a challenge to discipline and command authority, especially when the cold case begins to expose failures by officers and supervisors from an earlier era.
characters.name: Irvin Irving

characters.description: Bosch's former homicide partner, now working elsewhere in the department. Edgar is part of the professional life Bosch reenters, but reinstatement does not restore their earlier partnership or erase the years Bosch spent outside.
characters.name: Jerry Edgar

characters.description: A Los Angeles Times reporter familiar with Bosch and the department. The reopened murder has public interest as both a family tragedy and a test of whether new forensic evidence can correct an old investigative failure.
characters.name: Keisha Russell

recaps.ending: The new DNA result proves that Roland Mackey handled the gun used to kill Rebecca Verloren and breaks open the network the 1988 investigation failed to penetrate. Bosch and Rider establish that Rebecca's death grew out of racist intimidation directed at her interracial family and that people around Mackey concealed their parts afterward. Mackey's death during the renewed inquiry prevents a straightforward interrogation, but it does not stop the detectives from reconstructing how the weapon, abduction, and killing fit together and identifying the surviving responsibility behind the crime. The solution also shows how prejudice and divided attention weakened the original case, leaving Rebecca's parents to carry an uncertainty that should not have lasted seventeen years. Bosch and Rider deliver the truth to Robert and Muriel Verloren, though closure cannot restore their daughter or marriage. Bosch completes his first case after reinstatement and demonstrates that he can still work from within the LAPD. The return is not frictionless - Irvin Irving remains hostile - but Bosch finishes the book as a police detective again rather than a retired investigator borrowing access from others.
recaps.in_short: Harry Bosch returns to the LAPD after three years away and joins Kiz Rider in the Open-Unsolved Unit. Their first case is the 1988 abduction and shooting of sixteen-year-old Rebecca Verloren. Modern testing finds male blood on the murder weapon and matches it to Roland Mackey, whose racist background gives the old concern about an attack on Rebecca's interracial family new force. Bosch and Rider reinterview her separated parents, reconstruct the missing gun and the girl's private life, and review how the original detectives lost opportunities. Mackey dies as the current investigation closes around him, but the DNA and surviving records let Bosch and Rider establish his part and expose the group responsibility and concealment surrounding the killing. They finally give Robert and Muriel Verloren an answer, though not the life the unsolved case took from them. The closure validates Bosch's decision to return: despite conflict with command, he ends once again working as an LAPD homicide detective.

recaps.text: Previously: Harry Bosch left the LAPD after the Arthur Delacroix case convinced him that the department would protect a useful story over an uncomfortable truth. As a civilian he solved the Angella Benton cold case and learned that Eleanor Wish had raised their daughter, Maddie, in Nevada. While investigating retired profiler Terry McCaleb's final case, Bosch helped FBI agent Rachel Walling stop the serial killer called the Poet and began building a relationship with Maddie. The experience persuaded him that he still needed police work, and he applied to return to the LAPD.

Bosch is reinstated after three years away and assigned to the LAPD's Open-Unsolved Unit under Lieutenant Abel Pratt. His partner is Kiz Rider, an experienced colleague who knows both his strengths and the trouble that follows when he treats command as an obstacle. Their first file concerns Rebecca Verloren, a sixteen-year-old abducted from her home and found shot in 1988. A fresh examination of preserved evidence finds male blood on the murder weapon. A database match identifies Roland Mackey, giving the detectives a living lead that the original team never had. Before approaching him, Bosch and Rider rebuild the entire case so they can explain what the DNA means rather than mistake a laboratory match for a complete solution.

Bosch and Rider meet Rebecca's parents, Robert and Muriel Verloren, whose marriage did not survive the loss and the years without an answer. Rebecca was the child of a white father and Black mother, and the family received racist hostility in the community. Mackey's background and associations make that history immediately relevant, but the detectives keep other possibilities open while tracing the gun, access to the house, Rebecca's school life, and relationships she kept from her parents. The old file shows sincere effort mixed with missed connections and assumptions that hardened too soon. Bosch's return to the department also attracts Irvin Irving's attention, reminding him that a badge restores authority only inside a chain of command he once rejected.

Surveillance and background work place Mackey within a group shaped by white-supremacist loyalties and show that the DNA is consistent with more than casual contact. Bosch and Rider examine whether Rebecca was selected to punish an interracial family, whether the original plan was intimidation rather than murder, and who had possession of the weapon at each stage. Their renewed interest is noticed by people who believed the old case could never be reconstructed. At the same time, the detectives find that important leads were not pursued evenly in 1988. Racism was treated as one theory among many without the full network around Rebecca's family being mapped, and evidence that did not fit the early account lost urgency.

The inquiry closes around Mackey, but his death cuts off the direct interview Bosch and Rider hoped would establish the sequence and identify everyone involved. Rather than treating the dead suspect and DNA match as a convenient administrative closure, Bosch insists on proving how Rebecca left the house, why the family was targeted, and who helped move or conceal the weapon. The detectives return to the original witnesses and compare their current accounts with the 1988 record. Contradictions show that the killing was protected by shared silence and by the fragmented way the first investigation handled the racist group around Mackey. The case can still be closed, but only if the surviving evidence is made to carry more than Mackey's name.

Bosch and Rider connect the DNA evidence to the missing gun and the people who participated in the intimidation of the Verloren family. Mackey handled the weapon and had direct involvement, while others supplied opportunity, transport, or concealment. Rebecca's death emerged from the racist targeting of her family even where the participants later minimized their intention. The detectives also identify where the old investigation failed to press the network as a whole, allowing each person to present an isolated fragment and leaving no account strong enough for charges. Bosch's conflict with Irving intensifies as the findings reflect badly on the department's earlier work, but Rider helps keep the case within a form that can survive institutional resistance.

Bosch and Rider close Rebecca Verloren's murder by proving Roland Mackey's connection to the blood-stained weapon and reconstructing the racist intimidation, abduction, and concealment that surrounded her death. Mackey's own death prevents the simple ending of a confession and trial, but the evidence establishes his part and exposes the responsibility of the surviving people who helped the crime remain unsolved. The detectives give Robert and Muriel Verloren the answer withheld for seventeen years. It cannot repair their marriage or recover the years organized around uncertainty, but Rebecca is no longer only an open file. For Bosch, the case completes the arc begun when he surrendered his badge: he can challenge a false or incomplete institutional story while still working inside the department. Irving remains an adversary and the return carries constraints, but Bosch finishes as an active LAPD detective partnered with Rider.

characters.description: A socially isolated clerk and amateur butterfly collector who has watched Miranda from a distance for years. After winning a large sum of money, he buys a secluded country house and prepares its cellar in the belief that holding her there will eventually make her understand and love him. He narrates his actions in a flat, self-justifying manner and prefers possession and control to any relationship he cannot arrange on his own terms.
characters.name: Frederick Clegg

characters.description: A young art student whom Frederick abducts and confines in the cellar of his country house. Intelligent, observant, and determined to retain her identity, she tries negotiation, deception, escape, and appeals to his conscience. She calls her captor Caliban and insists that his gifts and claims of devotion cannot turn imprisonment into love.
characters.name: Miranda Grey

characters.description: Frederick's aunt, with whom he and her daughter have lived. The money Frederick wins allows Aunt Annie and Mabel to travel abroad, leaving him free to buy his isolated house without close family scrutiny.
characters.name: Aunt Annie

characters.description: Aunt Annie's daughter and Frederick's cousin. Her departure overseas with her mother removes one of the few people accustomed to Frederick's habits from his immediate life.
characters.name: Mabel

characters.description: An older painter who has become Miranda's friend, critic, and intellectual influence. In her diary she repeatedly measures her artistic ambitions and earlier behavior against his demanding opinions, while also examining the mixture of admiration, resentment, and attraction she feels toward him.
characters.name: George Paston

characters.description: Miranda's younger sister, recalled throughout the captive's diary as part of the family life from which she has been cut off. Miranda's memories of her are affectionate but also colored by ordinary sibling judgment and guilt.
characters.name: Minny Grey

characters.description: Miranda's father, a doctor whose conventional outlook she often criticizes in her private reflections. Her captivity leads her to reconsider both her distance from her family and the assumptions behind her earlier judgments of them.
characters.name: Doctor Grey

recaps.ending: After Miranda dies from an illness that Frederick failed to have properly treated, he buries her on his property. For a time he considers killing himself, but reading her diary lets him recast himself as the injured party because she never loved or respected him. He avoids accepting that his captivity and refusal to seek timely medical help caused her death. Returning to London, he notices another young woman, Marian, whose name and appearance remind him of Miranda but who seems less socially intimidating. He begins planning a new abduction, modifying his methods in light of what went wrong. The close shows that Miranda's death has produced no moral awakening: Frederick has converted it into experience for repeating the crime.
recaps.in_short: Frederick Clegg, an isolated clerk who collects butterflies, uses lottery winnings to buy a remote house and abduct Miranda Grey, an art student he has observed from afar. He keeps her in a furnished cellar, imagining that patience, gifts, and forced proximity will make her love him. Miranda resists through argument, manipulation, an attempted escape, and private writing that preserves her perspective and revisits her family, art, and relationship with the painter George Paston. Frederick treats her resistance as ingratitude and continually substitutes his fantasy of devotion for her stated wishes. When Miranda becomes seriously ill, his fear of exposure prevents him from obtaining adequate help, and she dies. He buries her and reads her diary, but uses its criticism of him to evade responsibility. Soon he selects another young woman and begins planning how to imprison her more effectively.

recaps.text: Frederick Clegg, a withdrawn municipal clerk and butterfly collector, has long watched art student Miranda Grey without approaching her. A large lottery win frees him from work and family oversight. He buys an isolated house, converts its cellar into a locked living space, abducts Miranda, and tells himself that once she knows him she will choose to stay. Miranda alternates between negotiation and resistance, demanding release and rejecting the idea that gifts can excuse captivity. She attempts to flee and tries to reach outsiders, but Frederick anticipates or defeats her efforts. His insistence on appearing gentle coexists with complete control over her movement, privacy, and access to help. Miranda eventually becomes dangerously ill. Frederick delays seeking a doctor because disclosure would expose him, and his limited measures fail. When he finally returns to the cellar after trying to obtain medicine, Miranda is dead.

Miranda's diary retells the captivity from inside the locked room and exposes the gulf between Frederick's account and her experience. She records practical escape plans, her attempts to understand and influence him, and her growing recognition that his idea of love leaves no room for her independent will. To keep her mind active, she revisits her life before the abduction: her ambitions as an artist, her discomfort with her privileged background, her family, and her intense friendship with the older painter George Paston. She subjects her own tastes and behavior to the same scrutiny she directs at Frederick. Moments when she pities her captor never alter her judgment that he must release her. As her illness worsens, the diary becomes fragmented. She remains hopeful that treatment or rescue will come, but her entries cease before either does.

Frederick discovers that Miranda has died. He initially imagines that the event has ended his own life as well and considers suicide, yet his response soon returns to concealment and self-protection. He places her body in a box and buries it in the garden, removing the immediate evidence of his crime. Reading Miranda's diary shows him how clearly she understood and disliked him. Instead of recognizing her account as proof of the harm he caused, he focuses on her private criticism and persuades himself that she was never worthy of the ideal he had created. This interpretation allows him to treat her death as a disappointment inflicted upon him rather than the consequence of abduction and neglected illness.

Frederick abandons the idea of suicide. Back in London, he watches a young shop assistant named Marian whose resemblance to Miranda attracts him, while her different social position makes her seem easier to manage. He begins thinking through a second abduction and decides that he can avoid his earlier difficulties by choosing differently and imposing stricter control. Miranda's death has not interrupted the pattern of collecting and possession; he has absorbed it as a practical lesson. The novel ends with Frederick preparing to repeat the crime, now with greater experience and no acceptance of responsibility for the woman buried at his house.

characters.description: A failed student of Unseen University, the Disc's college of wizardry, who was expelled after a single forbidden spell from the Octavo, the world's most powerful grimoire, lodged itself in his mind and crowded out every other. He can cast almost nothing and is a coward by conviction, treating flight as the only sane response to danger and mere survival as an accomplishment. He speaks a number of languages, which makes him useful as a guide. When the Patrician of Ankh-Morpork orders him to protect a visiting foreigner, his quiet, precarious life comes to an end.
characters.name: Rincewind

characters.description: A small, eager man from the wealthy Agatean Empire on the far side of the Disc, and the first tourist the Discworld has ever seen. An insurance clerk by trade, he travels for pleasure with a purse full of gold, an unshakeable belief that almost everyone he meets is good at heart, and a delight in danger he does not recognize as dangerous. He hires Rincewind as guide and interpreter and introduces Ankh-Morpork to the ruinous new idea of insurance.
characters.name: Twoflower

characters.description: A large travelling chest made of sapient pearwood, belonging to Twoflower. It walks on hundreds of little legs, follows its owner with doglike devotion, and holds far more than its size should allow, producing clean laundry from unknown depths. It is utterly loyal and utterly murderous toward anything that threatens its owner, swallowing enemies whole, and it cannot be stopped, reasoned with, or outrun.
characters.name: The Luggage

characters.description: The ruler of Ankh-Morpork, the Disc's greatest and most disreputable city. Shrewd and calculating, he grasps at once that a rich foreign visitor is both an opportunity and a diplomatic hazard, and he charges Rincewind with keeping the tourist alive and content, on pain of death.
characters.name: The Patrician

characters.description: The anthropomorphic personification of death, a robed skeleton who arrives in person to collect the souls of the notable and the interesting and speaks in a voice that lands directly in the mind. He takes a particular, repeatedly thwarted interest in Rincewind, turning up expecting to claim him only to be cheated each time by the wizard's improbable luck.
characters.name: Death

characters.description: One of the Disc's greatest heroes, a heavily muscled warrior who roams in search of treasure, monsters, and fame. Practical about his trade, he briefly takes Rincewind and Twoflower under his protection, drawn chiefly by Twoflower's picture-making box and the promise of reward.
characters.name: Hrun the Barbarian

characters.description: An ancient, malignant entity known as the Sender of Eight, a tentacled evil older than the gods that dwells beneath a lightless temple. Its power is bound up with the number eight, which wizards of the Disc avoid speaking aloud for fear of drawing its attention.
characters.name: Bel-Shamharoth

characters.description: A dragonrider and would-be ruler of the Wyrmberg, an inverted mountain whose people summon dragons out of imagination. Ambitious and commanding, she means to seize the Wyrmberg from her brothers and needs a champion to help her do it.
characters.name: Liessa Wyrmbidder

characters.description: The vast star turtle that swims through space carrying the four world-bearing elephants on its shell, with the Discworld resting upon them. Its age, its sex, and its destination are all unknown, and the question of where it is going underlies the whole of the Disc's cosmology.
characters.name: Great A'Tuin

recaps.ending: The Colour of Magic ends on a literal cliffhanger. Having escaped the scholars of Krull at the Rim of the world, Rincewind and Twoflower are swept over the edge of the Disc and fall, together with the Luggage, off the Rimfall waterfall and out into the void beyond the world. Nothing about their fate is resolved: they simply go over the edge and keep falling, with no rescue and no landing. The two remain bound together, the reluctant wizard and the relentlessly optimistic tourist, still pursued by the bad luck that has followed them the whole way. The larger questions of the setting are left open as well, chief among them the riddle the scholars of Krull hoped to answer, namely where the Great A'Tuin, the star turtle carrying the Disc, is swimming to and why. The story continues directly in the next book.
recaps.in_short: Rincewind, an incompetent and cowardly wizard of Ankh-Morpork, is ordered to protect Twoflower, the Discworld's first tourist, a naive and wealthy insurance clerk from the far Agatean Empire who travels with a fortune in gold and a homicidal walking chest called the Luggage. Their misadventures begin when Twoflower's talk of insurance burns Ankh-Morpork to the ground, and they flee the city with Death and other dangers close behind. They pass through a temple of the ancient evil Bel-Shamharoth, the Sender of Eight; visit the Wyrmberg, an inverted mountain of imaginary dragons ruled by the dragonrider Liessa; and are finally carried to the very Rim of the flat world, where the kingdom of Krull means to launch a ship over the edge and sacrifice them. Escaping, the two are instead swept over the Rimfall. The book ends with Rincewind and Twoflower plunging off the edge of the Disc into open space, their story left hanging.

recaps.text: In Ankh-Morpork the failed wizard Rincewind meets Twoflower, the Disc's first tourist, a cheerful insurance clerk from the distant Agatean Empire who has come to see the world and carries a fortune in gold and a walking chest, the Luggage. The Patrician orders Rincewind to guard the visitor and keep him alive. Twoflower's foreign notion of insurance quickly catches on, and when a tavern owner sets fire to his own premises to collect on it, the blaze spreads and consumes much of the city. Rincewind, who had meant to rob Twoflower and slip away, instead ends up fleeing the burning city at his side, pursued by trouble and by Death himself, who keeps arriving to collect the wizard only to be foiled.

Away from the city, Rincewind and Twoflower travel into wild country, unaware that their fates are literally being gambled over by the gods at a gaming table. They fall in with Hrun the Barbarian, a famous hero, and are drawn to a dark temple dedicated to Bel-Shamharoth, the Sender of Eight, an ancient evil tied to the forbidden number. Trapped inside, they barely survive an encounter with the creature and escape the temple.

The companions come to the Wyrmberg, an upside-down mountain ruled by dragonriders who conjure dragons out of their own imaginations. Twoflower, whose mind is vivid enough to summon a dragon of his own, is caught up in a struggle for control of the mountain between Liessa Wyrmbidder and her brothers, and Hrun becomes entangled in Liessa's schemes. Rincewind and Twoflower escape when their imagined dragons carry them off the mountain, and they fall clear of the Wyrmberg toward the Rim of the world.

The pair are carried to the very edge of the Disc, where the endless waterfall of the Rimfall pours off into space. They reach Krull, a kingdom perched at the Rim whose scholars intend to launch a great bronze vessel over the edge to learn the sex of the Great A'Tuin, and who plan to sacrifice the two travellers to the project. Rincewind and Twoflower escape, but in doing so are swept over the Rim. The book ends with them going over the edge of the world and falling into the void, their fate unresolved.

characters.description: An LAPD homicide detective defending a civil suit over his fatal shooting of Norman Church, the man police identified as the Dollmaker serial killer. Bosch remains certain Church was guilty, but a newly discovered victim forces him to test that certainty while he is on trial.
characters.name: Harry Bosch

characters.description: Bosch's girlfriend, a schoolteacher and the widow of narcotics detective Cal Moore. She wants a stable, honest relationship with Bosch but finds that his absorption in the Dollmaker case leaves little space for a shared life.
characters.name: Sylvia Moore

characters.description: The formidable attorney representing Deborah Church in the civil action against Bosch. Precise, aggressive, and highly prepared, she intends to prove that Bosch acted recklessly and then allowed the department to make Norman Church fit the Dollmaker case.
characters.name: Honey Chandler

characters.description: Norman Church's widow and the plaintiff in the lawsuit against Bosch. She presents her husband as a family man wrongly killed by police and seeks a public judgment against the detective who shot him.
characters.name: Deborah Church

characters.description: The man Bosch shot four years earlier after entering his apartment during the Dollmaker investigation. Evidence found afterward tied him to the murdered women, but the circumstances of the unarmed shooting now form the basis of the civil trial.
characters.name: Norman Church

characters.description: Bosch's homicide partner, who works the newly discovered killing while Bosch divides his attention between the investigation and the courtroom. Edgar supplies procedural balance to Bosch's more intuitive approach.
characters.name: Jerry Edgar

characters.description: The city attorney assigned to defend Bosch in the civil trial. He must counter Honey Chandler's presentation while managing a client who continues investigating during the proceedings and resists courtroom strategy.
characters.name: Rodney Belk

characters.description: Bosch's commanding lieutenant. Pounds expects the new homicide to be handled without disrupting the department's defense in court and has little patience for Bosch's refusal to separate the two matters.
characters.name: Harvey Pounds

characters.description: An LAPD vice detective who worked close to the world in which several Dollmaker victims lived. His access and private interests draw Bosch's attention as the team examines who could reproduce the killer's methods.
characters.name: Ray Mora

characters.description: A psychologist familiar with serial offenders and the Dollmaker investigation. Bosch consults him to understand whether the new burial points to Norman Church, an unknown partner, or someone copying confidential details.
characters.name: Dr. John Locke

characters.description: A senior LAPD official watching both the civil trial and the renewed murder inquiry. Irving's priority is preventing either from causing wider damage to the department.
characters.name: Irvin Irving

recaps.ending: Bosch determines that Norman Church really was the Dollmaker, but that a separate killer used Church's pattern for the woman buried in concrete and for later attacks. The copycat is psychologist John Locke, whose knowledge of the original investigation allowed him to reproduce details unavailable to the public. Locke kills Honey Chandler and attempts to complete another carefully staged murder before Bosch identifies and confronts him. Bosch kills Locke, ending the active threat. The solution preserves the central conclusion of the old police case without excusing the way Bosch entered Church's home and shot him. The civil trial ends without the sweeping condemnation Chandler sought, leaving Bosch legally able to continue but not untouched by the examination of his conduct. Sylvia has seen how completely the case consumes him and how little he can offer outside it; their relationship is badly weakened. Bosch closes one question about Church while carrying forward the professional and personal damage created by his methods.
recaps.in_short: Four years after Harry Bosch shot Norman Church, the suspected Dollmaker serial killer, Church's widow brings a civil case arguing that Bosch killed an innocent man and shaped the evidence afterward. During the trial, a note leads police to a woman's body sealed beneath concrete. She was killed after Church's death but bears private features of the Dollmaker crimes, raising the possibility that Bosch shot the wrong man or that someone else learned the pattern. Bosch and Jerry Edgar investigate while attorney Honey Chandler attacks the original case in court. The inquiry exposes Church's concealed life, draws suspicion toward people with access to victims and police information, and strains Bosch's relationship with Sylvia Moore. Bosch ultimately establishes that Church committed the original series and that a knowledgeable copycat committed the later murder. The copycat kills again before Bosch identifies and stops him. Bosch survives the civil case, but the investigation leaves another victim dead and his relationship with Sylvia close to collapse.

recaps.text: Previously: Harry Bosch solved the staged death of narcotics detective Cal Moore by following the black-ice drug route into Mexico. Moore had killed his half brother, substituted the body for his own, and assumed control of the brother's trafficking identity; he died when Bosch confronted him. Bosch then grew close to Moore's widow, Sylvia, and the two began a relationship. Bosch remains an effective LAPD homicide detective whose unauthorized methods keep him in conflict with Lieutenant Harvey Pounds and senior commander Irvin Irving.

Bosch goes to civil court over the shooting of Norman Church four years earlier. Police identified Church as the Dollmaker, a serial murderer who strangled women and altered their appearance, but Church was unarmed when Bosch entered his apartment and killed him. His widow Deborah, represented by Honey Chandler, argues that the department made the evidence fit after the fact. City attorney Rodney Belk defends Bosch, who resents being coached and remains certain Church was guilty. The trial reopens every weakness in the old investigation while Bosch tries to maintain his relationship with Sylvia Moore.

A message sent in the Dollmaker's style directs police to a woman's body buried beneath concrete. The killing occurred after Bosch shot Church, yet the body carries details that were never made public. Bosch and Jerry Edgar must consider several possibilities: Church was innocent, Church had a partner, or someone with privileged knowledge began copying him. In court, Chandler uses the discovery to strengthen her claim that Bosch acted first and justified himself later. Outside court, Bosch starts reconstructing the buried woman's identity and the period between her disappearance and the concealment of her body.

The buried victim's history leads the detectives through the sex trade and back toward people touched by the original Dollmaker investigation. Bosch confirms that Norman Church maintained a secret life his family did not know, supporting the old case even as the later murder remains unexplained. He consults psychologist John Locke about imitation and fixation and examines vice detective Ray Mora's access to victims and confidential information. Neither line yet proves who killed the woman in concrete. Sylvia grows frustrated that Bosch responds to the strain by withdrawing further into the case rather than trusting her.

Trial testimony exposes mistakes, assumptions, and damaging details from Bosch's confrontation with Church. Chandler is able to distinguish the evidence of Church's guilt from the question of whether Bosch followed lawful procedure when he shot him. The homicide inquiry likewise separates into two problems: who the Dollmaker was and who could copy his private signature afterward. Bosch follows a plausible suspect whose work and private conduct fit parts of the pattern, but the evidence does not account for every contact or message. The person behind the new killing remains close enough to developments in the lawsuit to exploit them.

Bosch clears away the strongest false lead and realizes that the copycat's advantage is not simply access to vulnerable women; it is expert knowledge of the Dollmaker evidence and of Bosch's thinking. The civil case reaches its final stage as both sides argue over whether Church's guilt can excuse the manner of the shooting. The active killer uses the attention around the trial to move again, placing someone central to the proceedings in immediate danger. Bosch must act before he has a complete courtroom-ready case, repeating the same tension between certainty and procedure that the lawsuit has examined.

Bosch identifies psychologist John Locke as the copycat. Locke's professional access to the Dollmaker material allowed him to reproduce facts that were withheld from the public and to direct suspicion toward other people connected with the victims. He kills Honey Chandler and attempts another staged murder before Bosch reaches him; Bosch kills Locke in the final confrontation. The evidence establishes two separate offenders: Norman Church committed the original Dollmaker murders, while Locke was responsible for the concrete burial and the renewed attacks. The civil verdict does not deliver the broad finding against Bosch that Deborah Church sought, although the trial has exposed the dangerous certainty with which he acts. Sylvia, exhausted by his emotional absence and total absorption in the hunt, draws away. Bosch ends the case professionally intact but with another death on the case and his closest relationship damaged.

characters.description: A capable nineteen-year-old sailor returning to Marseille as acting captain of the Pharaon. Honest, hopeful, and inexperienced in intrigue, he expects promotion and plans to marry Mercédès. His rapid good fortune arouses resentment among men he does not recognize as enemies.
characters.name: Edmond Dantès

characters.description: The honorable owner of the Pharaon, who values Edmond's conduct during the voyage and intends to confirm him as captain. He represents a prosperous Marseille shipping house and treats the young sailor with unusual trust.
characters.name: Pierre Morrel

characters.description: The Pharaon's supercargo, skilled with accounts and resentful of Edmond's expected promotion. He masks hostility behind practical questions while closely watching for a way to remove his younger rival.
characters.name: Danglars

characters.description: A neighbor of Edmond's father and an acquaintance of the returning sailor. Envious and often drunk, he recognizes the malice gathering around Edmond but lacks the resolve to oppose it.
characters.name: Gaspard Caderousse

characters.description: A young Catalan woman engaged to Edmond, steadfast in her love despite his absence at sea. Her beauty has also drawn the devotion of her cousin Fernand, whom she treats as a brother and firmly refuses as a husband.
characters.name: Mercédès Herrera

characters.description: A Catalan fisherman and Mercédès's cousin, consumed by jealousy of her engagement to Edmond. He has little talent for deception himself, but his desperation makes him receptive to suggestions from more calculating men.
characters.name: Fernand Mondego

characters.description: An ambitious deputy crown prosecutor in Marseille on the point of making a socially advantageous marriage. He initially examines Edmond as a routine political suspect and presents himself as a controlled servant of the restored monarchy.
characters.name: Gérard de Villefort

characters.description: Villefort's father, an experienced Bonapartist whom the royalist authorities regard as dangerous. His political identity conflicts sharply with the loyalist career and public name his son has constructed.
characters.name: Noirtier de Villefort

characters.description: An Italian priest and scholar imprisoned near Edmond in the Château d'If. Years of isolation have not dulled his disciplined mind: he knows languages, history, science, and strategy, and has patiently devised means to work beyond his cell.
characters.name: Abbé Faria

characters.description: The spirited son of General de Morcerf, traveling in Italy with his friend Franz d'Épinay. Privileged, curious, and confident that his family position will protect him, he readily pursues the adventures offered by Roman society.
characters.name: Albert de Morcerf

characters.description: A thoughtful young French aristocrat traveling through Italy with Albert de Morcerf. More cautious than his companion, he is intrigued and unsettled by the extraordinary wealth and secrecy surrounding a stranger known as Sinbad the Sailor.
characters.name: Franz d'Épinay

characters.description: A feared Roman bandit chief who commands an organized network outside the law. He is capable of violence but observes his own agreements and treats the mysterious Count of Monte Cristo with marked respect.
characters.name: Luigi Vampa

characters.description: The Count of Monte Cristo's Corsican steward, reserved and intensely loyal. He manages the Count's new household at Auteuil and carries a personal history connected to the property.
characters.name: Bertuccio

characters.description: A young Greek woman living in the Count's household, treated by him as a protected companion rather than a servant. She is the daughter of Ali Pasha of Janina and carries memories of her family's overthrow and enslavement.
characters.name: Haydée

characters.description: Pierre Morrel's son, now an honorable army officer devoted to his family. He remembers the unknown benefactor who once saved the Morrel firm and approaches the Count with gratitude and trust.
characters.name: Maximilien Morrel

characters.description: Villefort's gentle daughter by his first marriage, closely protected by her grandfather Noirtier. Her family expects her to make a suitable match, while she privately loves Maximilien Morrel.
characters.name: Valentine de Villefort

characters.description: A polished young man presented to Paris as an Italian nobleman and the son of Major Cavalcanti. His pedigree is vouched for by documents and wealth, making him attractive to the status-conscious Danglars family despite his unfamiliar background.
characters.name: Andrea Cavalcanti

recaps.ending: Benedetto's trial publicly exposes Villefort as the father who tried to bury him alive. Villefort returns home to find that Héloïse has poisoned herself and their young son Édouard; the accumulated catastrophe destroys his sanity. The Count, horrified by the child's death, accepts that his vengeance has exceeded any authority he possessed. Danglars, the last principal conspirator, is captured by Luigi Vampa and forced to spend nearly all his fortune on food before the Count reveals himself and grants him pardon. Mercédès begins a modest new life in Marseille, Albert enters military service, and the Morcerf fortune is abandoned. Valentine, secretly saved from poisoning by the Count, is reunited with Maximilien after he has been tested to the edge of despair. Having settled his fortune and made restitution where he can, the Count leaves with Haydée, whose love offers him a future beyond revenge. He leaves Maximilien and Valentine with the counsel to endure uncertainty and retain hope.
recaps.in_short: Sailor Edmond Dantès is falsely accused by Danglars, Fernand, and Caderousse on the eve of marrying Mercédès. Prosecutor Villefort suppresses proof of his innocence to protect his own career, and Edmond spends fourteen years in the Château d'If. Fellow prisoner Abbé Faria educates him and reveals a treasure on Monte Cristo. After escaping and finding the fortune, Edmond returns as the mysterious Count of Monte Cristo. He rewards the Morrel family and constructs elaborate downfalls for his enemies, now wealthy and powerful in Paris: Fernand is exposed as a traitor and kills himself; Caderousse and Villefort's household are destroyed by crimes the Count sets in motion; Danglars is ruined and captured. Innocents also suffer, especially Villefort's young son, forcing the Count to question his claimed role as providence. He ultimately pardons Danglars, saves Valentine for Maximilien Morrel, and departs with Haydée, leaving revenge behind for a possible new life.

recaps.text: In 1815, nineteen-year-old Edmond Dantès returns to Marseille aboard the Pharaon and is promised its captaincy by the shipowner Morrel. He plans to marry Mercédès, but his advancement and happiness provoke three men: Danglars envies his promotion, Fernand wants Mercédès, and Caderousse resents his good fortune. A denunciation devised by Danglars accuses Edmond of carrying a Bonapartist letter. Deputy prosecutor Villefort initially sees that Edmond is politically innocent, then discovers the letter is addressed to his own Bonapartist father, Noirtier. To protect his royalist career, Villefort destroys the letter and sends Edmond without trial to the Château d'If. Napoleon's brief return and defeat reorder France while Edmond remains forgotten. His father dies in poverty, Mercédès disappears from his reach, and Morrel's attempts to help fail.

After years of despair, Edmond hears another prisoner tunneling nearby and meets Abbé Faria. The scholar educates him in languages, history, science, manners, and political calculation, then reconstructs the conspiracy that caused his imprisonment. Faria also reveals the location of the Spada family treasure on the island of Monte Cristo. When the priest dies after repeated seizures, Edmond takes his place in the burial sack and is thrown into the sea, escaping after fourteen years in prison. He joins smugglers, reaches Monte Cristo, and finds the immense fortune exactly where Faria described it. Now wealthy and transformed, he begins investigating the people from his former life. Disguised as Abbé Busoni, he hears Caderousse confess how Danglars, Fernand, and Villefort destroyed him and how his father died, while also learning that Morrel alone tried to save him.

Edmond confirms the prison record and secretly rewards his few loyal friends. When Morrel's shipping firm collapses, an unknown benefactor settles its debts, restores a lost vessel's value, and saves the family from ruin at the last moment. Years later, the story moves to Italy, where the immensely rich Count of Monte Cristo cultivates mystery around his identity. Franz d'Épinay encounters him during the Roman carnival, and Albert de Morcerf is abducted by Luigi Vampa's bandits. The Count secures Albert's immediate release, creating a debt of gratitude. Albert introduces him to Parisian society and to the families now formed by Edmond's enemies: Fernand is the celebrated Count de Morcerf and Mercédès's husband, Danglars is a banker, and Villefort is a powerful crown prosecutor. The Count arrives with unlimited credit and the social access needed to begin his concealed design.

The Count establishes an Auteuil house whose past alarms his steward Bertuccio. Bertuccio explains that years earlier he stabbed Villefort there and found a newborn child whom Villefort had tried to bury; the child survived and grew into the criminal Benedetto. The Count also meets his enemies' households, including Villefort's wife Héloïse, and discusses poisons with her in terms that encourage her existing interest. He manipulates Danglars with enormous financial credibility and displays horses and wealth that draw the banker into competition. Haydée, the daughter of the deposed Ali Pasha of Janina, lives under the Count's protection and possesses knowledge connected to Fernand's past. Meanwhile, Maximilien Morrel, son of the shipowner Edmond saved, loves Villefort's daughter Valentine in secret. The Count treats the Morrels with genuine warmth while positioning the other families around the Auteuil property and its buried history.

Several plots converge around marriage and inheritance. Héloïse hopes her son Édouard will inherit Villefort wealth that would otherwise pass to Valentine. Valentine and Maximilien remain devoted to each other, while Valentine's grandfather Noirtier resists her proposed marriage to Franz d'Épinay. Though paralyzed, Noirtier communicates and changes his will, then reveals his responsibility for the death of Franz's father, ending the match. The Count introduces Major Cavalcanti and the supposedly noble Andrea Cavalcanti, giving Danglars a more prestigious prospective husband for his daughter Eugénie than Albert. Andrea is actually Benedetto, placed in society under a purchased identity, though the families courting him do not know it. The Count also engineers a false telegraph message that causes Danglars a large market loss. At a dinner in Auteuil, he tells a story about an infant buried in the garden, terrifying Villefort and Madame Danglars, who share the secret.

The Count's pressures begin breaking the alliances among his targets. Danglars abandons Albert as a match for Eugénie in favor of Andrea Cavalcanti. In the Villefort household, members of Valentine's maternal family die after taking poisoned drinks, and suspicion grows without yet settling on the true poisoner. Noirtier's precautions protect Valentine. Evidence of Fernand's betrayal at Janina reaches the newspapers: he sold out Ali Pasha, then profited while Haydée and her mother were enslaved. Albert first treats the report as an insult against his father and asks Beauchamp to investigate. Haydée is prepared to testify from personal memory and documents. The Count appears to let each exposure arise independently, preserving his public position as benefactor and guest while the histories he assembled begin to destroy reputations, fortunes, and marriage plans.

Haydée testifies before the Chamber of Peers and proves Fernand betrayed her father and sold his family. Publicly disgraced, Fernand is abandoned by Albert and Mercédès. Albert challenges the Count, believing him responsible, but Mercédès recognizes Edmond and privately begs him to spare her son. Edmond agrees to die rather than kill Albert. Learning the deeper truth from his mother, Albert apologizes at the duel. Mercédès and Albert renounce Fernand's fortune and leave; Fernand confronts the Count, recognizes Edmond, and kills himself. The result gives Edmond his revenge but leaves Mercédès grieving and dispossessed. Elsewhere, Caderousse discovers Andrea's criminal identity and tries to profit from it, while the poisonings inside Villefort's family continue. The Count's interventions are no longer confined to the guilty men and increasingly place people he values near the consequences of his plan.

Caderousse attempts to rob the Count and is fatally stabbed by Benedetto while escaping; before he dies, the Count reveals that Edmond Dantès survived and confronts him with his choices. Andrea's identity collapses on the eve of his marriage to Eugénie, who leaves Paris with her companion Louise. Danglars steals liquid assets from his bank and flees. Héloïse is exposed as the poisoner in Villefort's home. Valentine appears to die, devastating Maximilien, but the Count has recognized the danger, substituted a controlled drug, and secretly removed her from the grave. He prevents Maximilien's suicide and demands a month of trust without revealing that she lives. Benedetto's trial then exposes Villefort as his father. Villefort returns home to find Héloïse and Édouard dead by her hand and loses his reason. Horrified by the child's death, the Count sees that his vengeance has gone beyond justice. He has Danglars captured by Vampa, but ultimately pardons him after stripping away most of his fortune. Valentine is restored to Maximilien, and the Count leaves with Haydée, choosing the possibility of love over further punishment.

characters.description: Heir to Illéa and, with her mother gravely ill and her father unwilling to leave her side, acting regent. She is running a country in unrest, a Selection she can no longer treat as theater, and a family missing a brother, all at once. The cold self-sufficiency she began with has been worn down: she now knows she needs people, which she finds harder to manage than governing.
characters.name: Eadlyn Schreave

characters.description: Queen of Illéa, recovering from a heart attack brought on by her son's elopement. She came to the palace as a Five in her husband's Selection and has spent her reign softening the monarchy; she is now too weak to do much of anything, and the household is arranged around her.
characters.name: America Schreave

characters.description: King of Illéa, who abolished the caste system twenty years ago and has spent his reign managing the consequences. With his wife's life in danger he hands the day-to-day rule of the country to his daughter and refuses to be moved from America's side.
characters.name: Maxon Schreave

characters.description: Eadlyn's twin brother, now living in France with Princess Camille after eloping without warning. His absence is a wound in the family and a political problem, and he and Eadlyn are still repairing what he did.
characters.name: Ahren Schreave

characters.description: Eadlyn's younger brother, thoughtful and steady, and more use to her in a crisis than she had ever assumed a younger sibling could be.
characters.name: Kaden Schreave

characters.description: One of the six remaining Selected, raised inside the palace and a fixture in Eadlyn's life since childhood. He wants to design buildings rather than hold a title, and he is honest with her in a way almost nobody else at court risks being.
characters.name: Kile Woodwork

characters.description: Kile's younger sister, who grew up in the palace and has spent her life behaving as though a crown were owed to her. She is a persistent irritation to Eadlyn and rather less secure than her performance suggests.
characters.name: Josie Woodwork

characters.description: Eadlyn's maid and, though it took Eadlyn a long time to admit it, her friend. She tells the princess uncomfortable truths and keeps her steady while the palace is in crisis.
characters.name: Neena

characters.description: One of the remaining Selected, a young man of Finnish descent whose enthusiasm survives everything and who still speaks almost no English. He cooks, he is entirely sincere, and every word between him and Eadlyn passes through his translator.
characters.name: Henri Jaakoppi

characters.description: Henri's translator, present at every conversation between Henri and the princess and, by virtue of not being a candidate, the one person at the palace with nothing to gain from her. Eadlyn finds his company easier than anyone's, which is an increasingly awkward fact.
characters.name: Erik

characters.description: One of the remaining Selected, good-humored and far more interested in design and tailoring than in politics.
characters.name: Hale Garner

characters.description: One of the remaining Selected, composed and unsentimental, who treats the competition as a negotiation rather than a courtship and is frank with Eadlyn about what an arrangement between them would and would not be.
characters.name: Ean Cabel

characters.description: One of the remaining Selected, warm and openly affectionate, and one of the men Eadlyn came to like before she was prepared to like any of them.
characters.name: Fox

characters.description: The son of August and Georgia Illéa, who led the Northern rebels a generation ago and helped bring down the caste system. Confident, media-friendly, and popular with exactly the people the palace has failed to reach, he offers Eadlyn his family's goodwill and his public support at a moment when she badly needs both.
characters.name: Marid Illéa

recaps.ending: Eadlyn refuses the marriage that would have been most useful to her and makes the choice she actually wants. She exposes what the Illéas were doing, releases the remaining Selected without humiliating any of them, and tells Kile and Henri the truth to their faces rather than through an announcement. Then she goes on live television and tells the country that she has chosen Eikko, Henri's translator: not one of the Selected, not titled, not the political asset her advisers would have picked. In the same period Maxon and America step down, Maxon abdicating so that he can care for his wife and give his daughter the throne outright rather than a regency, and Eadlyn is crowned queen of Illéa. Ahren and Camille return from France, and the breach in the family is closed. America recovers. Eadlyn ends the book as a young queen who has learned to rule by being trusted rather than obeyed, married to a commoner she chose openly, with the monarchy intact and the country's confidence in it restored.
recaps.in_short: With her mother recovering from a heart attack and her father refusing to leave the queen's side, Eadlyn Schreave is made regent and must run Illéa while finishing the Selection she never wanted. Six young men remain, and this time she cannot treat them as scenery. She grows closer to Kile, to the irrepressible Henri, and above all to Erik, Henri's translator, who is not a candidate and therefore not permitted to matter. Marid Illéa, son of the rebel leaders who helped end the caste system, offers her his family's popularity and a public alliance, and Eadlyn takes it before discovering that the Illéas intend to replace the monarchy with themselves at the head of an elected government, and that her courtship is the lever. She exposes them, releases the Selected honestly, and announces on live television that she has chosen Eikko, a commoner with no title at all. Maxon and America abdicate, Eadlyn is crowned queen, and Ahren and Camille come home.

recaps.text: Previously: twenty years after King Maxon abolished Illéa's caste system, the country is in unrest, because money and old prejudice have quietly done the work the castes used to do. Maxon also changed the succession so that his firstborn would inherit regardless of gender, making his daughter Eadlyn the first woman named heir. Cold, controlled, and uninterested in marrying anyone, Eadlyn agreed to hold a Selection of her own purely to distract the country. Thirty-five young men came to the palace, among them Kile Woodwork, who had grown up there and whom she had never liked. She treated the whole thing as theater, staging a kiss for the press and dismissing a candidate who handled her roughly, but the men refused to remain props: she came to like Kile, warmed to the guileless Henri, and found herself looking forward to conversations with Erik, Henri's translator, who was not a candidate at all. Then her twin brother Ahren, tired of being overlooked, eloped to France with Princess Camille, leaving a letter warning Eadlyn that the succession now rested on her alone. The shock brought on their mother's heart attack, and the previous book ended with the queen's survival unknown.

Queen America survives, but she is seriously ill and needs surgery and a long recovery, and Maxon will not leave her. He hands the running of the country to Eadlyn, who becomes regent in everything but name. Six of the Selected remain in the palace while she takes on a workload she has been trained for but never carried alone, in a country still angry about the failures of the post-caste settlement and now unsettled by a prince who left. Ahren writes from France; Eadlyn is not ready to forgive him. The Selection, which she began as a distraction, has become an obligation she cannot postpone, because the throne needs a settled succession and she is now the whole of it.

Ruling makes Eadlyn better at the Selection rather than worse at it. She stops staging and starts asking the remaining men what they would actually do with a position at her side, and finds their answers genuinely useful. Kile talks to her honestly about the life he wants, Henri's cheerfulness is a relief in a grim household, and every conversation with Henri necessarily includes Erik. Neena keeps her upright, her brother Kaden proves steadier than she expected, and Josie is a constant irritation. Eadlyn also begins to see how much of the country's anger is directed at a palace that has not listened, and she starts looking for a way to reach the people her family lost.

Marid Illéa approaches the palace. The son of August and Georgia Illéa, the Northern rebel leaders who helped bring down the castes a generation ago, he is charming, comfortable with the press, and popular with exactly the citizens the crown has failed to reach. He offers Eadlyn his family's goodwill and a public alliance, and the pairing is instantly successful: the coverage is warm, the protests quieten, and Eadlyn is credited with mending a historic rift. She is aware of how useful he is to her and treats the arrangement accordingly. At the same time she is aware that the person she is happiest talking to is Erik, who has no title, no place in the Selection, and no business being considered at all.

Eadlyn narrows the field further, and does it decently. When two of the remaining Selected turn out to be in love with each other, she releases them quietly rather than exposing them, and other men leave for reasons of their own. Her feelings for Erik become impossible to explain away, and she has no framework for them: a queen is expected to marry a candidate, an ally, or an asset, and he is none of these. Her mother's slow recovery, her father's exhaustion, and the constant weight of governing leave her increasingly clear about what she actually values and increasingly aware of how little of it the Selection was designed to deliver.

The Illéas' real intentions surface. Marid's family does not want a marriage into the monarchy; they want the monarchy replaced by an elected government with themselves at the head of it, and Marid's courtship of Eadlyn has been a means of positioning that argument in public. Eadlyn realizes she has been used as a stage prop in her own capital, exactly as she once used the Selection. It is a hard lesson in what she has been doing to other people, and it forces her to decide what the crown is actually for and whether she can defend it on any grounds other than inheritance.

Eadlyn moves against the Illéas' plan and settles the Selection on her own terms. She stops calculating which marriage would be most useful and admits, to herself and then to the people it concerns, that she loves Eikko. She is honest with Kile, who has wanted a life outside the palace all along, and with Henri, whose translator she has fallen for. What she has learned as regent has changed the question she is answering: not who would make the best consort for the throne, but what kind of queen the country would actually trust, and whether she is willing to be that in public.

Eadlyn exposes what the Illéas were attempting, releases the remaining Selected without humiliating any of them, and then goes on live television to tell the country that she has chosen Eikko, Henri's translator, who holds no title and was never a candidate. Maxon and America step down, Maxon abdicating so that he can care for his wife and hand his daughter the throne outright, and Eadlyn is crowned queen of Illéa. Ahren and Camille return from France and the family is whole again; America recovers. Eadlyn marries the man she chose, having learned to rule by earning trust rather than demanding obedience, with the monarchy intact and the country's confidence in it rebuilt.

characters.description: A seventeen-year-old mortal raised in the High Court of Faerie by the man who murdered her parents. Stolen out of the human world as a small child alongside her twin, Taryn, and their half-fey older sister, she has grown up in the household of Madoc, the High King's grand general, with every comfort and no safety: she can be enchanted, she cannot lie, and the fey children she studies beside despise her for being human. Stubborn and combative, she trains with a sword, answers cruelty with defiance rather than retreat, and wants the one thing her adoptive father will not take seriously: a knighthood and a place at court that would make her impossible to dismiss.
characters.name: Jude Duarte

characters.description: Jude's twin sister, raised beside her in Madoc's household. Where Jude answers the court's hostility with defiance, Taryn believes survival lies in giving the fey no reason to notice her at all: she keeps her head down, avoids provoking Cardan's circle, and intends to marry into Faerie and be safe. She urges Jude to stop fighting battles she cannot win, and she has a suitor of her own whose name she refuses to say.
characters.name: Taryn Duarte

characters.description: The eldest of the three sisters and the only one who is half fey, with split-pupilled cat eyes and the ability to enchant mortals. Madoc is her father, which is why he took all three girls when he destroyed the rest of their family. She refuses to accept Faerie or the man who raised her, spends as much time as she can in the human world, and keeps a mortal girlfriend there who does not know what she is.
characters.name: Vivienne

characters.description: A redcap and the High King's grand general: a war-loving fey soldier who killed Jude's mother, once his own wife and long since fled from him, along with the human man she had married, then carried all three of their daughters back to Faerie and raised them as his own because his sense of honour demanded it. He is affectionate, indulgent and entirely unrepentant, teaches Jude swordwork, and treats her ambition to be knighted as a child's passing fancy. He loves battle for its own sake.
characters.name: Madoc

characters.description: Madoc's fey wife, pale-skinned and white-haired, who joined the household after the mortal girls did and has never trusted them. She fears they are a danger to her small son and keeps them at a careful distance while observing every courtesy of family life.
characters.name: Oriana

characters.description: Oriana's young son, a small horned fey boy who adores his older sisters and is indulged by the whole household. He is kept well away from the court and its politics.
characters.name: Oak

characters.description: The youngest son of the High King of Elfhame and the cruellest of the court's young nobles, with a tail he keeps hidden under his clothes and a talent for making an audience of everyone present. Landless, disregarded by his own family and given no duties, he spends his time drinking, staging revels and tormenting whoever is easiest to torment. He reserves a particular and unexplained hatred for Jude.
characters.name: Cardan

characters.description: A princess of the Undersea and daughter of its queen, fostered at the High Court and one of Cardan's closest companions. Beautiful and contemptuous, she considers mortals beneath notice and takes an active part in making the Duarte sisters miserable.
characters.name: Nicasia

characters.description: A young fey lord in Cardan's circle and the most physically dangerous of them. Where the others humiliate the mortal sisters for sport, he escalates, and he does not appear to need an audience.
characters.name: Valerian

characters.description: A fey lord with fox-red hair and amber eyes, one of Cardan's companions but the only one who takes no obvious pleasure in the group's cruelty. Playful and hard to read, he is drawn to drama for its own sake and begins seeking Jude out, offering her the kind of attention no one at court has offered her before.
characters.name: Locke

characters.description: The High King's second son and his chosen heir, poised and outwardly gracious, expected to be crowned at the coming coronation. He keeps a private company of spies and assassins, and he takes an interest in Jude, seeing a use for a mortal willing to bind herself to his service.
characters.name: Prince Dain

characters.description: The ageing High King of Elfhame, who has ruled for centuries and now means to pass the crown to one of his children and step down. Remote and visibly tired of governing, he presides over a court whose quarrels no longer seem to interest him.
characters.name: High King Eldred

characters.description: A pale, quiet fey archer, the marksman of the small band of spies Jude joins. He is the most patient of the three and the one who takes on her training when she needs a steady hand rather than a lesson in cunning.
characters.name: The Ghost

characters.description: An explosives expert with a cloud of white hair, one of the three spies Jude works alongside. Cheerful and practical, she treats a lethal craft as a trade like any other and is generous with what she knows.
characters.name: The Bomb

characters.description: A green-skinned hob and the most experienced of the spies, a thief and lockpick who teaches Jude to open what is locked and to move through the palace unseen. He is blunt about the odds a mortal faces in their line of work.
characters.name: The Roach

characters.description: The High King's eldest son and master of Hollow Hall, a controlling and violent figure who keeps a household of enchanted mortal servants and has custody of his youngest brother, Cardan. Passed over for the throne, he makes little secret of believing himself the better claimant.
characters.name: Prince Balekin

recaps.ending: Jude breaks Madoc's plan by making Cardan an offer he cannot refuse: she will put him on the throne, and in exchange he swears to obey her for a year and a day. Oak, as Prince Dain's son and an heir of the blood, sets the crown on Cardan's head before the court, and Cardan's first commands, every one of them Jude's, undo the coup. Balekin is stripped of his standing and imprisoned in the Tower of Forgetting. Madoc loses his post as grand general and is put out of the palace, outplayed by the mortal daughter he trained and half-admiring of how she did it. Jude sends Oak to the human world to be raised by Vivi and her mortal girlfriend, Heather, keeping the true heir out of every faction's reach until he is old enough to rule without a keeper. Taryn stays in Faerie, engaged to Locke, the breach with her sister unhealed. Cardan sits on the throne of Elfhame as a king nobody expected and nobody trusts, resentful of the leash and unreadable about Jude herself. Jude holds no title anyone would name, only a secret: for a year and a day the High King of Faerie must do as she says, and the clock has already started.
recaps.in_short: Jude Duarte and her twin, Taryn, are mortal girls raised in the High Court of Faerie by Madoc, the fey general who murdered their parents. Despised at court for being human, Jude wants a knighthood and a place no one can take from her; her chief tormentor is Cardan, the High King's youngest son. To gain power of her own she swears herself to Prince Dain, the king's chosen heir, and becomes one of his spies, learning lockpicking, poison tolerance and courtcraft while Cardan's circle escalates from humiliation to attempted murder. Jude kills one of them in self-defence, discovers that the boy courting her has been courting Taryn at the same time, and falls out with her sister. At the coronation the eldest prince, Balekin, murders the High King and most of his heirs, and Madoc is revealed as his ally. Jude gets hold of Cardan, the only remaining heir who can pass the crown, and learns that her small brother Oak is secretly Dain's son and the true heir Madoc intends to rule through. She crowns Cardan instead, on the condition that he obey her for a year and a day, and sends Oak to the human world for safety.

recaps.text: Jude Duarte and her twin, Taryn, are mortals raised in the High Court of Faerie. When they were small, a redcap warrior named Madoc came to their family's house, killed their mother, who had once been his wife and had fled him, killed the human man she had married, and then carried all three of the daughters, including his own half-fey child, Vivienne, back to Elfhame to raise. Ten years on, Jude and Taryn take lessons with the children of the gentry, who despise them for being human. The worst of their tormentors is Cardan, the High King's youngest and least regarded son, with his companions Nicasia, Valerian and Locke. Jude wants a knighthood and a place at court; Madoc, indulgent in everything else, refuses to treat the ambition as real and suggests she would be safer in the mortal world. Taryn wants only to be inoffensive enough to marry into Faerie without incident, and Vivi wants all three of them to leave. At a revel, Cardan's circle forces Jude to eat enchanted fruit, which strips away her self-control and leaves her dancing and weeping for their amusement while the court looks on.

Determined to be something other than a target, Jude goes looking for power. Prince Dain, the High King's chosen heir, offers it: he keeps a private company of spies, and if she swears herself to his service he will knight her once he is crowned. Jude accepts and is bound to him, joining the Court of Shadows, three fey agents known as the Ghost, the Bomb and the Roach, who begin teaching her to pick locks, to fight without honour and to gather what is said at court. To make herself harder to kill and harder to control, she takes small daily doses of faerie poisons to build a tolerance. The realm is preparing for High King Eldred's abdication and Dain's coronation, and Madoc, as grand general, is busy with the arrangements. Locke, alone of Cardan's circle, starts seeking Jude out, and Taryn, who has a suitor of her own she will not name, warns her sister that provoking the gentry will get her killed.

Jude works as Dain's spy, listening at revels and reporting what the gentry say about the succession. Locke's pursuit of her becomes open enough for the court to notice: he brings her to his family's estate, dresses her in finery and enjoys the discomfort her presence causes, and Jude cannot tell whether his interest is genuine or a performance staged for an audience. Cardan's hostility sharpens as Locke's attention grows.
